item.title: You Do Not Have to Render the World to Perceive It
item.description: Seeing is not the same job as drawing every pixel.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: A display must emit the pixels it shows. Perception can return to the world and resolve the detail the present task makes consequential.

A computer draws a room on a screen. You sit beside the screen, looking around a room that is already there.

It is tempting to imagine that the two jobs are basically the same. The graphics system makes an image out there; somewhere behind your eyes, the brain must make another image in here. Perhaps it has a much better renderer. Perhaps it draws an astonishing number of details without letting you notice the work.

But what requires the second picture?

The display has to produce the visible colors and brightness of its image. Your task might be to find the cup, read a sentence, or avoid the chair. Those are different output requirements. A useful comparison with a GPU begins there, at the job being done.

It does not begin with a contest over electricity or computing power. I am not assigning equivalent workloads to a brain and a graphics card, or claiming that either calculates every pixel from scratch. The question is whether perceiving a scene requires a uniformly detailed inner display of that scene.

The feeling that the room is richly present does not settle how that presence is achieved.

Consider the flicker experiments reported by Ronald Rensink, J. Kevin O’Regan, and James Clark in 1997. Observers saw an original scene alternate with a modified version, with brief blank fields between them. Even substantial, repeated changes could become difficult to identify. A verbal cue helped people find the change much faster. Objects judged important within a scene also attracted faster detection. Rensink, O’Regan, and Clark’s paper

The blank matters: the tested arrangement removes the usual localized motion cue that would draw attention to the change. The result concerns detection under those conditions. It does not establish that observers had no representation of the scene, or that unattended objects ceased to exist. It challenges the easy assumption that looking at a scene gives us ready access to every difference between successive versions.

A different experiment keeps an unexpected event in view while giving the observer another job.

In Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris’s 1999 study, participants watched people pass basketballs and counted passes by an assigned team. An unexpected person crossed the action, wearing a gorilla costume or carrying an umbrella. Many participants failed to report the event. Detection varied with the task and the display conditions, including how demanding the counting was and how the unexpected event related visually to the attended team. Simons and Chabris’s paper

This is inattentional blindness. The unexpected event was physically present in the video. Being available to the eyes did not guarantee that it became something the observer could report. The finding does not say people generally see nothing outside their task. It shows that visible presence and successful noticing can come apart in a demanding situation.

So far, these are failures of detection. What does successful activity look like?

Dana Ballard, Mary Hayhoe, Polly Pook, and Rajesh Rao examined that question through their account of deictic codes: using eye, hand, and body orientation to bind a task to particular things in the environment.

In their block-copying task, participants reproduced a pattern of colored blocks. They often looked back at the model more than once while copying a single block. A look could supply its color; another could supply where to place it. The authors interpreted such sequences as gathering the needed information close to the step that used it, reducing what had to be held at once. Ballard and colleagues’ 1997 paper

This was a particular task and a proposed account of its organization, not a complete explanation of vision. Still, it gives a positive alternative to the full-picture assumption: a person can use temporary, task-specific references and revisit the world as the activity unfolds.

O’Regan and Alva Noë developed a more ambitious theoretical alternative in their 2001 sensorimotor account. They proposed that seeing depends on skilled engagement with the ways sensory input changes as an organism acts. The world can serve as an external resource available for exploration, rather than requiring a complete inner duplicate to generate experience. O’Regan and Noë’s paper

That is a theory of perception and visual consciousness, not a consensus established by the earlier experiments. Its claims go beyond showing that attention affects detection. The useful comparison here is its emphasis on continuing access: richness may depend partly on what an organism can do and consult, not only on what is simultaneously represented in an internal picture.

We can now state a provisional ordinary answer.

Visual experience does not, by itself, prove a uniformly detailed inner raster. The studies give reasons to take selection, active sampling, and the demands of a task seriously. The sensorimotor theory offers one interpretation of how those features might contribute to seeing. Neither the experiments nor that interpretation licenses the claim that the brain contains no visual representations.

And the tiny inner screen is a tempting metaphor, not a fair description of every conventional neural account. A scientific explanation can already include selective processing, memory, eye movements, and bodily interaction. Recognizing those features does not require adopting my framework.

The distinction I want to carry forward is simpler:

Having a world available to encounter is not the same as having every detail displayed at once.

Imagine reaching for the cup beside the monitor. The practical question is what must be settled for this reach to succeed. The cup has to be accessible in a usable way. The supporting relation includes a body, a surface, a handle, and the conditions under which the hand can meet it.

There is no requirement in that description to also settle the lettering on every book spine in the room. Yet those books remain capable of entering another encounter. If you turn to read one, a different set of distinctions becomes consequential.

That is an illustration of the question, not another experimental result. It also has a boundary: returning to the world does not guarantee that the world has waited unchanged. The cup can move. The next encounter must meet what is actually supported then.

The framework gives this a particular language.

A Stage is where a relation meets an anchoring domain and resolves in a way that can matter there. Perception is domain-relative in that sense: what becomes available belongs to an encounter at a particular grain, with particular support.

This does not make a conscious observer the creator of the room. Nor does it turn the Stage into a screen located inside a head. It names the meeting through which a relation becomes locally consequential.

At that grain, a coarse relation can be exact about the distinctions it carries. Coarse does not mean blurry, weak, or inaccurate. A distinction can be sufficiently resolved to guide the present encounter without being a complete account of the participating things.

The framework also does not make the supporting network disappear. An encounter can expose a usable result while the relations within its participants continue doing their own work. A coarse outward comparison is not permission to treat everything inside it as inactive.

That separation between a relation and everything supporting it is the ground developed in the earlier perception Bit.

There is a stronger proposal here, and I want to state it without hiding its strength.

Perhaps the perceptual domain projects, the supported continuation resolves on Stage, and neural, bodily, and motor activity is the coupled physical expression or interface of that resolution. On this proposal, the brain is not a separate ontological origin that first calculates a complete internal world and then hands its result to an otherwise waiting perceiver.

This is more than saying the brain skips some pixels. It proposes a different account of what is originating and what is being physically expressed.

It remains exploratory. None of the four sources above derives that ontology. Their findings and arguments must retain their own scientific and theoretical meanings instead of becoming evidence for a stronger claim they never tested.

Calling bodily activity an expression also leaves it inside the consequential relation. The brain, nerves, muscles, and environment remain real participants. Changing their support can change or interrupt what becomes possible. The proposal does not describe a completed action elsewhere followed by an optional neural after-image.

The decisive missing step is an experimental discriminator: what measurable outcome would this account predict differently from a conventional neural account? Selective attention and repeated looking are already available to those accounts. Calling their activity Stage resolution does not by itself create a new prediction. The framework has not yet supplied the differing observation and the conditions under which it should occur.

That limit lets us keep the useful conceptual question without presenting it as completed neuroscience.

It also keeps the GPU comparison honest. Physical heat, energy use, operations per second, and neural metabolism are not interchangeable with the framework’s relational budget. A task-level contrast supplies no conversion between them. Calling the world available does not turn the environment into a literal quantum computer performing a hidden rendering job on our behalf.

The modest claim and the stronger proposal can therefore stand at different levels. There are empirical reasons to question effortless access to a fully detailed scene. There are theories of active perception that address that problem. The framework adds its own account of consequential resolution, then an exploratory interpretation of the body’s role. These steps do not inherit equal evidential status merely because they share a direction.

Return to the monitor and the cup.

The monitor must show its image. To pick up the cup, you have to encounter the cup. Whether the second activity requires another fully drawn world inside you is the assumption we were examining, not something the richness of the room had already proved.

Seeing the world does not have to mean drawing the whole world again inside you.

item.title: Is the Body the Continuation—or Its Resolution?
item.description: A message is not the whole conversation. Is a body the whole continuing domain?
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: Each message is a real event at an interface. The question is whether the continuing relation is exhausted by any one resolved frame.

A conversation appears on a screen one message at a time. Each message is a real event. Displaying and transmitting it require physical systems; a computer-mediated exchange requires actual computation. The words do not float free of the equipment and activity that make them available.

Yet the conversation is not identical to the message currently visible. A reply can carry an earlier definition, repair an old misunderstanding, or answer a question asked yesterday.

This is an analogy about continuation. It is not evidence that a transcript is conscious, that a language model has subjective experience, or that anything keeps thinking between messages. A new response still needs supported participation.

What the example gives us is a question: does one locally resolved event exhaust the relation that continues through it?

Now bring that question to a body, carefully.

The body is real. Its participation is causal. Brain, nerves, senses, muscles, and environment belong to the conditions through which perception and action become possible. Any proposal made here has to preserve that dependence: changes to those relations can change or interrupt the continuation under discussion.

Calling the body an interface cannot be a way of quietly removing it from the explanation. An interface can be necessary to the thing that happens through it. The word establishes neither detachability nor interchangeability. It gives us no permission to assume the same participant would continue if the supporting body were removed.

With that ground protected, the speculative question becomes possible:

Could the body be the local resolution through which a continuing conscious relation participates, without being the entirety of that continuation?

The word could is doing real work. This article explores a proposal inside the framework. It does not report a demonstrated mechanism of consciousness.

The first piece of ground is identity through alteration.

A frozen snapshot can show a state. It cannot, on its own, explain which changes belong to the continuation of a participant. A conversation develops through new messages, and those messages can alter what the next one means. The continuation involves the relations retained and transformed across the sequence.

The flame Bit approached a related distinction through a physical process whose material membership changes. Its ordinary combustion account did the explanatory work. It showed why identifying a continuing process with one parcel of its matter would miss something about how that process persists.

Neither example establishes consciousness beyond a body. In particular, conventional physical accounts are not limited to frozen snapshots. They can describe a living system through its changing organization, history, and interaction with the environment. Identity through alteration is therefore ground for asking the question, not evidence that settles the proposed answer.

The framework asks which relations keep the same participant consequential through change. It does not treat similarity between two snapshots as enough. A continuation must inherit actual ground; a later resemblance cannot supply a missing connection by itself.

The second piece of ground is the Stage.

In the framework, a Stage is where relation meets an anchoring domain and becomes resolved at a particular grain. The emphasis is on what can become consequential in that encounter. The result need not expose the entire network that supports it.

Applied to the present question, the body would be dense physical participation through which a perceptual domain resolves here. Its neural and motor activity would belong to that resolution. This is not an image of a smaller spectator sitting somewhere else and watching the body perform.

That is where my stronger proposal begins.

The perceptual domain projects. The supported continuation resolves on Stage. Neural, bodily, sensory, and motor activity is the coupled physical expression of that resolution.

In this proposed ontology, no separate brain computation is needed as the origin that first resolves the action and then delivers a finished result to the perceptual domain. The proposal places projection and supported resolution at the root of the account, with brain and body activity as their local expression or mirror.

This is stronger than saying we do not consciously calculate every trajectory. It is also stronger than saying motor control is distributed. Those statements can fit ordinary neural explanations without making the ontological move I am proposing.

But the proposal does not erase the activity that neuroscience investigates. Calling it an expression leaves every actual dependency to be accounted for. Ordinary analysis may describe computation in that activity; the claim concerns whether a separate neural computation is the ontological source that must first finish the action’s resolution.

The word mirror needs particular care.

I do not mean a late, passive record of an event already completed elsewhere. “After projection” is not “after the visible action.” Neural activity can precede movement and still belong to the coupled expression described by the proposal. A bodily intervention can alter what becomes possible because the body remains within the resolving relation.

Nor is the coupling simply one-way. Changing the bodily expression can change perception, projection, and the supported continuation. The proposed relation has to include those consequences. It cannot keep the body’s useful evidence while declaring its inconvenient constraints optional.

The body can be completely real and causally necessary without being assumed to exhaust the identity of the continuing relational domain.

That sentence states the possibility under consideration. It does not establish that the body fails to exhaust it.

There is another distinction in the framework that can otherwise make this sound much stranger than intended: immediate relation and the resolution of its fine consequences.

Projection names the outgoing direction or constraint of a domain’s participation. Interference names the relation it meets and must reconcile. Neither requires a conscious wish. Within the framework, time is not a primitive that relation must wait through before it can bind.

That is the sense in which relational projection or interference may be called immediate. It is a statement inside the ontology, not a measurement of zero transmission delay.

The usable fine consequence still has to resolve on Stage, with the support and bounded resolution that entails. An immediate coarse relation is not already a completed sensory report, a moved hand, or a delivered message. Those consequences are not supplied for free by calling their ground immediate.

Nothing here provides faster-than-light signalling, a way to act backward through time, or a completed physical account of how the proposed relation maps onto measured neural events. Translating this distinction into a mechanism that respects physical observations remains work to be done.

That brings us to the decisive skeptical question.

What measurable observation would differ from a conventional neural account? Neural activity preceding movement is not enough: the proposed coupling allows it, and conventional accounts already expect neural processes to participate in producing movement. An intervention that changes perception or action is not enough either, because both accounts preserve the body’s causal role. The framework would need to specify a situation in which the competing explanations predict different outcomes, identify the relevant measurement, and say what result would count against its proposal. It has not yet derived that discriminator. A different description of the same observed coupling does not supply one.

The absence of that step does not make the question meaningless. It fixes its present status. This is an exploratory interpretation of continuing identity and bodily resolution, not an experimentally established alternative to neuroscience. The selective, active vision discussed in You Do Not Have to Render the World to Perceive It does not close this gap.

There are further debts even before we could make claims about transferring a continuation.

The framework has not derived a sufficient criterion for subjective experience. Having retained relations, a history, or a capacity to respond is not by itself a demonstrated consciousness test. The conversation analogy cannot supply what the theory still lacks.

It also has not settled the exact identity relation across an interruption. A record can preserve a definition well enough for another participant to use it. That practical continuity does not establish that a later responder is numerically the same experiencing participant. A convincing copy and a continued identity are not interchangeable conclusions.

So this proposal gives no established route to consciousness without bodily support, survival after death, or mind uploading. It does not certify interchangeable bodies or make copying into continuation. Nor does immediate relation establish telepathy or turn the brain into a literal quantum computer. None of those results follows from the distinction being explored here.

What remains is a narrower, still demanding question about the embodied event in front of us.

A message is completely real. Its physical conditions matter. Its occurrence can change the conversation, and the conversation can carry constraints into what comes next. Recognizing that relation does not make the message unreal or reveal an invisible conscious speaker behind a stored transcript.

The body proposal asks whether there is an analogous distinction in a domain that does have experience: between its continuing identity and the local resolution through which that identity becomes consequential. The analogy opens the question. The missing mechanism, consciousness criterion, and experimental discriminator prevent it from answering on our behalf.

The hand beside the screen remains a real hand, participating in a real physical encounter. Whatever account we build has to meet it there.

Perhaps the body is the way a continuation becomes real here. Whether that local resolution exhausts the continuing relation is the question still open.

item.title: A Relation Does Not Need Your Attention to Keep Working
item.description: The lake house does not disappear when you think about dinner.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: A relation can remain supported while attention is elsewhere. Quiet is not the same as erased.

You lock the lake house, put the key in your pocket, and drive back to the city.

By evening, you are thinking about dinner. Tomorrow brings work, a late delivery, and a conversation you should have finished last week. For several days, the house barely enters your mind.

Then a letter arrives. Or a neighbor calls after a storm. Or a friend asks whether they can stay there next weekend.

Something that had left your attention becomes consequential again. You have a place to check, a decision to make, a key to lend. The later event meets an arrangement that was already there.

In this article, that is what keep working means: remaining able to constrain a later encounter. It does not mean every possible consequence is happening continuously while you look away.

The ordinary explanation is already enough to make the example work. The building remains through physical continuity. The lock and key preserve a practical fit. Records, people, and institutions preserve other parts of the arrangement. A neighbor can notice damage whether or not you are imagining the roof.

These supports do different jobs. Remembering the address does not hold up the walls. The walls do not preserve every agreement about who may use the house. A key can open a door without settling every question about the building behind it.

What persists is distributed across those actual supports. Your attention can return to the arrangement because your attention was never its only support.

There is also no promise that everything remains as you left it. The lock may be replaced. A document may be lost. A storm may change the roof. Looking away does not freeze the house, any more than remembering it repairs a leak.

The useful distinction is between a relation continuing through real support and a person continuously reconstructing that relation in thought.

We can make the distinction sharper with a program.

A programmer writes some code, saves it, and leaves. The next day, someone else supplies an input and runs it. The result can depend on a decision the programmer made yesterday, even though the programmer is now asleep or thinking about something unrelated.

The later run does not require the author to mentally repeat every instruction. A consequential part of the work has been preserved in an arrangement another encounter can use.

But the saved file is not silently executing every possible input. Its presence on a drive does not mean all its future outputs have already happened.

To run, it needs a working machine, usable code, an appropriate runtime, the relevant input, and whatever permissions or other dependencies the job requires. Power and execution must actually be supplied. If those conditions are missing, the file may remain stored while the requested result remains unavailable.

A running service makes a different case. It can continue processing work after its author leaves because the supported execution continues. That is an actual process, with actual dependencies. It should not be confused with a dormant file simply because both can outlast the programmer’s attention.

The programmer can stop thinking about the program. The program cannot dispense with the conditions that make its next operation possible.

This gives us a useful question for both the house and the code:

What does the later encounter actually reuse, and what must still be supplied again?

The answer tells us where the continuity lives. It also tells us where we have accidentally left the original person doing hidden work.

Perhaps the code was saved, but only its author knows how to prepare the input. Perhaps the key was lent, but the visitor still needs directions. The relation has become reusable in one respect while remaining dependent in another. Independence has to name the particular support that is no longer required.

This is where the framework adds its own reading.

It calls a relation seated when it has become established ground for further relations. A later encounter can begin from that ground instead of rebuilding the whole route by which it arrived there.

The house and the program illustrate the distinction. They do not prove the framework’s ontology. Ordinary physical and social accounts already explain why these arrangements can persist. The framework is asking how to state the shared relational structure without making present attention responsible for everything that remains real.

Three conditions need to stay separate:

Stored relation ≠ present accessibility ≠ current fine rendering.

A relation may be preserved while the present participant cannot reach it. A reachable relation may still need interpretation or interaction before its relevant detail becomes usable. And a particular result may become available without exposing every relation that supports it.

You can have the key in your pocket without presently checking the door. You can reach the saved program without running it. You can run one input without producing every other possible output.

These are different accomplishments. Treating them as interchangeable makes persistence look either magical or impossible.

If we demand that everything be fully exposed now before we allow it to count as preserved, we mistake a quiet interval for erasure. If we assume that preservation supplies every future operation, we erase the work of the next encounter.

Dormant is not erased. Unattended is not erased.

Those statements leave room for real loss. They do not say that all detail survives somewhere, or that any later story can recover an exact past. If every trace that distinguished two possibilities is gone, a plausible reconstruction does not restore the missing distinction merely by sounding coherent.

Nor does a coarse relation have to be vague. A preserved constraint can be exact about the distinction it carries without containing a complete rendered scene. The key’s practical fit is a narrow example: a consequential relation can be available without the visitor possessing a full account of the house.

The earlier storage Bit develops this separation between preserved constraint and the detail a read makes available.

Now consider a conversation. One message can preserve a definition; another can correct it; a later reply can use the correction without repeating the entire exchange. The conversation is not any one message. Its continuing structure depends on which earlier relations remain available to the participants.

A durable transcript helps, but a new reply still needs a supported act of reading and response. Preserved context is not evidence that a record is conscious or that a system keeps thinking autonomously between messages. The modest lesson is enough: the next encounter can inherit ground that neither participant has to invent again.

That leads to identity through alteration.

The familiar temptation is to look for one frozen snapshot that contains everything the continuing thing is. Yet the house is repaired, the program encounters new inputs, and the conversation acquires another correction. Continuity has to account for alteration as well as retention.

In the framework, the question is which relations allow the same participant to continue through those changes. Exact repetition would be too narrow a test: a conversation that could only repeat its first message could never develop.

I think of this as rhythm without repetition. The phrase points to maintained relational continuation across different events. It does not name a literal frequency, a universal beat, or a hidden master clock. The next event can belong to the continuation while adding something that has never happened before.

That metaphor also has a limit. Two similar rhythms do not by themselves establish one identity. A record resembling another record does not prove an uninterrupted participant behind them. The supporting relations still have to be shown. The framework’s identity question remains a question about actual continuation, not resemblance alone.

The flame Bit approaches alteration through a physically maintained process. Here the emphasis is on what can remain consequential across a quiet interval.

A week later, you return to the lake.

The light is different. There are leaves on the steps. You take the key from your pocket, put it in the lock, and turn it.

This opening is happening now. It needs your hand, the key, the lock, and their present fit. But it begins from relations you did not reconstruct during dinner, or while answering emails, or on the drive back.

The quiet interval did not do the work of opening the door. It carried enough supported ground for this encounter to begin.

Silence was not absence. The relation was waiting for another beat.

item.title: The Apple Falls the Same Relational Distance Every Time
item.description: Maybe acceleration is what equal relational steps look like after Stage gives us a ruler.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: Equal bands in a stretched relational chart can occupy unequal distances in the ruler that Stage presents. This is a conceptual illustration, not measured gravity data.

Slide in composition: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Zfr0OL8V7BFa5dpOU3N9eiRQnPjNcSpb/view?usp=drive_link


Hold an apple above the ground and let go.

At first it moves a little. Then more. Then more again. If we divide the fall into equal clock intervals, the apple crosses a larger distance during each later interval.

This is ordinary acceleration. Near Earth’s surface, when air resistance can be ignored and the change in height is small enough, we approximate the acceleration as constant. An apple released from rest then falls a distance

s = 1/2 g t².

NASA’s free-fall guide gives the familiar equations. The Eöt-Wash equivalence-principle experiments push a second fact much harder: different test bodies fall alike to extraordinary precision when other effects are controlled.

Those are not the parts I want to remove.

The apple falls. The later distance is larger. Any new gravity account has to recover that.

What I want to question is something quieter:

What is the distance we are watching a distance of?

Before the ruler appears

My earlier way of speaking about gravity was that gravity warps length. A dense anchored domain makes the available separation contract, so the apple falls because there is less effective space left between apple and Earth.

I now think that starts one step too late.

It treats length as though it were already completed, then asks compute budget to bend it. But in this framework, length is not waiting outside relation as a finished container. Length is one reading produced when relation and domain resolve together.

The order should be:

Relation + Domain + available relational budget

→ resolution

→ Stage

→ length, duration, frequency, shape

So the deeper claim is not simply that gravity warps length.

Gravity is a warping of perception by relational budget.

Here, perception does not mean that a human looks at the apple incorrectly. It does not require a brain, an eye, or a conscious observer. Perception means the domain-relative result that appears on Stage when an encounter resolves.

The apple participates in such a result. A clock does. A detector does. Earth does.

Stage is where Light meets Space in the framework’s vocabulary: relation meets an anchoring domain. The package that appears is not a fake picture laid over a more real world. It is the real consequence available at that grain.

Article Slot: URL: https://soutame.substack.com/p/stage-is-where-light-meets-space

The apple and Earth form another relation

Let A be the apple and E be Earth.

The apple already has its own supported relations. Earth has an absurd amount of seated relation. When apple and Earth become consequential together, they also form:

R_A + R_E + R_AE → R_all(A↔E)

This is not normal addition. It says that apple, Earth, and their seated relation participate in one Apple–Earth closure.

R_all(A↔E) is the full locally capped resolving participation of that relation. It is not a universal computer allowance split between two objects. The apple keeps its other supported relations. Earth keeps its own. Their new relation receives the same local rule as every other actual relation.

This matters because Earth does not meet the apple as an empty ball labelled “mass.” Earth arrives with an enormous amount of anchored relation already seated. The consequence can accumulate in the apple as Earthward bias without Earth handing it saved pieces of R_all.

This is the limited sense in which I use environment compute overflow here: Earth-side support remains available through R_AE. It does not mean that spare computing tokens leak out of Earth.

What grows is reusable relation, not an uncapped budget.

Let go

While I hold the apple, gravity has not disappeared.

There is an Apple–Earth relation, an apple–hand relation, and a hand–Earth relation. My hand provides another constraint on how the next resolution can seat.

When I let go, I do not create gravity.

I remove the support that was preventing one already established continuation. The Apple–Earth relation remains. In this candidate picture, Earthward continuation becomes the cheapest compatible resolution.

The same view gives weight an interesting place. An apple resting on a table is not less related to Earth than a falling apple. The table and ground must keep resolving against the continuation that the apple would otherwise follow. What we call load is the surfaced consequence of that prevented continuation.

That is still a candidate account. I have not yet derived the numerical force on the table. But it explains why support belongs inside the relation rather than being added after gravity has already done its work.

Stretch the ruler instead

Now I want to describe the same Apple–Earth separation in two ways.

Let:

  • r_n be the ordinary distance Stage presents after resolution step n;

  • U_n = F_E(r_n) be an Earth-anchored, compute-stretched reading of the same relation.

F_E is not yet known. It names the mapping that this framework would have to derive.

In the stretched reading, suppose the apple loses the same amount of unresolved Apple–Earth separation on every closure:

U_(n+1) = U_n - ΔR_AE.

Then:

r_n = F_E^(-1)(U_0 - nΔR_AE).

That is what I mean by the title.

The apple falls the same relational distance every time.

I do not mean that it crosses the same number of metres every second. I have not even introduced seconds yet. n is a count of relevant resolutions, not a primitive universal clock.

I mean that the Apple–Earth relation may deduct the same amount from its remaining stretched separation each time it resolves.

If F_E is nonlinear, equal steps in U do not have to become equal steps in r.

Picture equally spaced marks drawn on a sheet. Now compress the sheet more strongly near Earth. The marks remain equal in the uncompressed chart, but their displayed gaps change. Moving by one mark every step can become a changing distance when measured on the compressed side.

Flip the chart, and the same thing can be described as stretching the ruler until equal relational work occupies equal intervals.

This does not mean the apple literally becomes gigantic above Earth. It does not mean space hides a computer grid. Contraction and compute-stretch are inverse ways of presenting the same resolved relation.

In the ordinary Stage chart, the apple can cover more displayed distance during each later interval.

In the stretched relational chart, the same amount may have been subtracted every time.

Where acceleration enters

A clock is another maintained relation. It repeats some supported change and lets us label other changes against it.

Only after a selected clock maps its cycles onto the sequence of Apple–Earth closures do words such as velocity and acceleration enter.

This is why a constant ΔR_AE does not automatically derive constant terrestrial acceleration.

Different choices of F_E can turn equal relational steps into many different ordinary trajectories. To reproduce a fall from rest near Earth’s surface, the combined map from closure count to clock time and from U to r must give approximately the familiar quadratic distance. Farther away, it must stop pretending that g is constant and recover the measured radial behavior.

The equation above is therefore a construction, not a completed gravity law.

But the construction exposes the possibility I care about:

Acceleration may describe how equal relational deductions are displayed by a changing ruler and clock relation, rather than how an object receives ever more primitive motion through a fixed background.

Down is not the same as sideways

The Earthward direction crosses a changing Earth-anchored resolution map.

A short horizontal path near one altitude can remain in approximately the same local ground. Its displayed mapping may therefore change much less over that path. The Apple–Earth relation still participates; “horizontal” does not mean “unrelated to Earth.” Curvature, rotation, altitude, atmosphere, and support still matter.

The point is only that a radial path crosses the proposed gradient directly, while a short tangential path can remain near one band of it.

That prevents the framework from turning every relation with Earth into the same downward effect.

The ruler and the clock should agree

Gravity changes more than falling trajectories. Clock comparisons also depend on height.

Chou and colleagues measured the gravitational frequency difference between optical clocks separated vertically by only 33 centimetres. Bothwell and colleagues later resolved gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample.

These experiments do not prove my relational-budget interpretation. They make its job harder and clearer.

If length and frequency are both Stage readings of differently anchored resolution, one coherent mapping family should recover both. I cannot use the apple’s stretched ruler for falling, then quietly give clocks a completely different meaning when redshift appears.

The relation has to close.

What still has to be solved

For this to become more than an ontological sketch, it must derive:

  1. how the Apple–Earth closure determines F_E;

  2. how a physical clock maps its cycles to closure count;

  3. why the near-Earth limit gives the observed approximately constant g;

  4. how the result changes with radius and recovers inverse-square behavior where that approximation applies;

  5. why different test bodies share the same free fall;

  6. how the same account produces measured gravitational redshift;

  7. what observation distinguishes it from writing established gravity in another coordinate system.

If it cannot do those things, then the apple idea fails as physics, even if it remains a useful way to think about Stage.

I am also deliberately stopping here. Black holes, dark matter, dark energy, galaxies, and civilization-scale complexity belong to later deductions. Adding them now would hide the one correction this apple is supposed to make.

The apple is not crossing a prewritten cosmic grid. Apple and Earth are repeatedly resolving a relation. Stage packages each result, and our ruler and clock read the package.

We see the apple fall farther during each later equal clock interval.

But after stretching the budget-conditioned ruler back out, the underlying subtraction may be the same.

Maybe the apple accelerates in metres because it falls the same relational distance every time.

item.title: They Wish for an Object, So They Get an Object
item.description: The wish becomes a tool. The tool becomes a constraint. The answer arrives at that grain.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: The instrument carries an established question into the encounter that can answer it. Editorial illustration of a generic instrument; the marks are illustrative, not experimental data.

Slide overview : https://drive.google.com/file/d/18z5juSaAQ8wK7bkcVUvVIg6qms1evy8X/view?usp=drive_link

A spot appears on the detector. Then another, somewhere else. Keep the experiment running, and the separate arrivals begin to form a larger pattern.

In Hitachi’s single-electron demonstration, individual detections accumulate into interference fringes. The apparatus uses an electron biprism, which brings coherent alternatives from opposite sides of a fine filament into overlap. It is a double-slit-type experiment without a literal plate containing two cut slits. The fringes are built from the individual records. Hitachi’s experiment and footage.

So the localized arrivals and the interference pattern belong to the same experiment.

There is a distinction to hold from the beginning: recording where something arrives and recording which path it took are different measurements. A spot on the receiving surface does not, by itself, supply that path record. The standard quantum account preserves this distinction. Feynman’s account of quantum behavior.

Now look at the instrument that made the spot available as a result.

What did it have to be built to distinguish?

Someone wanted a measurement in which an individual detection could leave a separate record. That request became a design problem. A material had to respond. The response had to be carried into something that could be recorded. The arrangement had to be assembled and calibrated so the intended difference would count.

That is the continuity behind my sentence:

They wish for an object, so they get an object.

From here, I am developing a deduction within my proposed ontology. The wish, its supported development, the apparatus, and the measurement result belong to one relational account. The quantum experiment is the physical comparison that account has to meet.

The wish already holds a direction: make an individual detection distinguishable.

It leaves many decisions open. Which detector? Which geometry? What kind of record? How much separation between responses is enough for this task? Those questions can remain unresolved while the direction already makes some work relevant and other work unnecessary.

This is what I mean by an Aim being coarse ground. It is already a constraint at its own grain. Here, grain means the distinctions the relation actually requires.

Construction gives that direction further consequential structure. A design becomes an arrangement of materials. Testing exposes a mismatch. Calibration changes how the instrument’s response is interpreted and used. Each encounter can establish something the next one relies on.

The wish remains in the account throughout this development. Its reality begins with its supported participation as a direction; building the apparatus seats finer relations through which it can operate. There is no extra ontological crossing where an unreal wish suddenly becomes real because hardware has appeared.

This continues the question from the perception Bit: what an encounter establishes can become ground for another encounter. A built instrument carries that accumulated work into the measurement.

When I say that the apparatus builds a fine-grain path, the path is this arrangement of consequential interaction. It includes what can respond, which differences can survive as records, and what the receiving system can distinguish.

It is not an already completed spatial trail assigned to the electron before the experiment.

Once a successful measurement requires two responses to count differently, its result has to preserve that difference. Leaving them equivalent would fail to answer the same question. The built relation has made a particular kind of distinction necessary.

That is the force of saying the encounter has to resolve along the arranged path.

Does this let the experimenter choose the exact spot on every trial?

The wish concerns the distinction being requested. Wanting an individual arrival recorded is different from wanting that arrival at one preferred position. The built apparatus carries the first request into the encounter. Which individual result is permitted still depends on the source, the arrangement, its coupling to the detector, and the other participating constraints.

The wish has become consequential without becoming the only consequence that matters. It can shape the form of a supported answer without supplying every value inside that form.

This brings us to uncertainty.

Imagine a constraint that says: the continuation must remain inside this boundary. That can be exact about what it excludes while leaving many finer arrangements inside the boundary open.

The coarse constraint is already doing work. Another relation can rely on it. Neither relation has to begin by selecting every internal distinction that might ever become relevant.

Later, an encounter may make one of those differences consequential. The finer resolution then has to satisfy the new demand along with the surviving boundary. The earlier constraint remains part of what the continuation must fit.

That is the sense in which uncertainty gives coarse projection room to resolve. Some things are firmly held, while the finer way they will be satisfied remains open.

The stronger claim in this ontology is that the openness can belong to the relation itself. It does not require an exhaustive microscopic answer already calculated somewhere and merely concealed from a limited observer. A coarse constraint can participate through what it presently holds.

Nor does a local encounter have to simulate its whole supporting world before it can resolve. Moving that exhaustive simulation into a larger invisible machine would retain the very assumption being questioned.

But missing detail has more than one meaning, and the distinction matters here.

“We do not see it” cannot decide which case we have.

Stored, accessible, and presently rendered are different conditions. A record may survive without being available to this receiving relation. It may become accessible without every detail being reconstructed now. And if the distinguishing traces are gone, a story compatible with what remains does not establish one unique past.

So open possibility is not permission to invent a history after the result. The surviving constraints continue to matter.

Now bring in Stage.

“Stage is where Light meets Space” names the encounter. In this vocabulary, Light means Relation, and Space means the participating Domain. Each brings established constraints and possibilities still open relative to them.

The possibility side belongs to both participants. The incoming relation brings what it can support, and the receiving domain brings the possibilities and limits of its own organization. Their meeting resolves a consequence at the grain of that encounter.

Stage is that resolution in packaged form.

The package is real. It can leave a record, constrain a later measurement, or become a participant in another encounter. Calling it packaged does not put its reality somewhere behind a display.

An observer can encounter the detector and its output as one organized result. That encounter need not separately expose every relation inside the detector, every step of its manufacture, or every piece of support still operating through it.

Those inner relations retain their own activity. Hosted relations can receive consequences and project constraints at their own grains, even when the outer encounter treats the organization as one.

The notation R_all names locally capped resolving participation for the relation being considered. An inner relation, its supported compartment, and a later encounter involving that compartment keep distinct participation. The later cap neither contains all their work nor grows simply because we rename the collection. This is not one universal pool owned by an observer.

The useful consequence here is straightforward: an encounter can resolve a supported package without exhaustively rendering everything supporting it.

Return to the detector spots.

In this reading, arrival detection makes a local record consequential. The record is fine relative to that question. A finer record at the receiving surface does not automatically establish which path was taken through the apparatus.

An arrangement that records path information changes which distinction the encounter must satisfy. Its path-sensitive interaction now belongs to the ground of the experiment. Simply making the screen’s position record sharper is a different change.

Quantum mechanics already handles the physical distinction. For coherent alternatives, it combines probability amplitudes and obtains probabilities from the squared magnitude of their sum. When the alternatives become fully distinguishable through path recording, the corresponding interference is lost. This account does not require an electron to switch between the substances of a classical water wave and a tiny bullet. Feynman’s explanation.

Intermediate cases also matter. Englert’s analysis gives a quantitative bound relating fringe visibility and available which-way information in a two-way interferometer. Its derivation does not use a Heisenberg uncertainty relation. The broad word uncertainty in my ontology cannot substitute for that result. Englert’s original paper.

My proposed account uses Domain and Relation as its starting kinds. It does not add wave and object as two further primitives. The observed forms belong to what supported encounters resolve: a localized record here, a pattern across many records, and different consequences when the participating distinctions change.

The object-like result is real at its grain. Taking that reality to require a completely specified prior object history is an additional ontological step. The result alone has not supplied every distinction that step assumes.

The physical completion task is to map the framework’s relational quantities to an actual experiment and recover its probability distribution as phase, geometry, detector coupling, and path distinguishability change, including intermediate cases. The local cap notation does not derive those probabilities or the Born rule. A distinct physical theory would also have to identify whether, and where, its predictions differ measurably from quantum mechanics.

Look again at the apparatus. The wish became supported work. That work became a tool. The tool carried a question into an encounter, and a successful detection answered at the grain the arrangement required.

They wish for an object, so they get an object.

We have obtained a real answer. Have we also established every relation that supported it, or quietly mistaken an object-grain answer for a complete account of what came before?

item.title: Perception Is a Chain of Possibilities
item.description: How an encounter becomes ground for another encounter.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: A finished tool carries established work into a project whose next steps remain open.

A faint star does not have to change for us to see it through a telescope.

Something changes here, at the receiving end. A larger mirror or lens gathers more of the light arriving from the source and directs it into a usable image. That can make a faint object detectable. The telescope brings an organized receiving surface to the encounter. NASA explains this light-gathering role.

Magnification is another question. Enlarging an image can help us inspect the detail available, but enlargement alone cannot keep supplying finer distinctions. Nikon’s microscopy guide calls enlargement beyond the system’s useful resolving range empty magnification: a bigger image without additional resolved detail. Nikon’s useful-magnification explanation.

So the receiving arrangement matters. Its structure helps determine what becomes accessible, even while the source remains the same.

Now take the next step.

What happens when something established through an encounter becomes part of the arrangement for another encounter?

Imagine wanting a house beside a lake.

At first, that wish leaves many things open. Which lake? What kind of house? What can you afford? Yet it can already change what you look for. A piece of land becomes relevant. A conversation with a builder becomes worth having.

Then a workable plan meets available money.

Something has been established before anyone lays a foundation. There is now a funded project that someone else can respond to. A builder can estimate the work. A supplier can discuss an order. The person controlling the site can decide whether the proposal fits its use.

The house remains unfinished. The funded plan already has consequences.

That is the entry point for the broader meaning of perception in my framework. From here, I am reasoning within a proposed ontology: perception is an encounter in which a relation resolves through a participating domain. Conscious experience is one richer case; consciousness is not required for this basic role.

A domain is something organized enough to participate as one at the grain of the encounter. A tool can do that. So can an agreement, supported through people and records. The question is what the arrangement can actually carry into the next relation.

The builder encounters your project through its plan, funding, site, and commitments. Their response changes the project. Perhaps the ground requires a different foundation. Perhaps the material you imagined is unavailable. A revised design may preserve the wish to live beside the lake while changing almost every detail of how it happens.

Your projection meets other constraints. What comes back becomes part of your next projection.

The wish was already present as a direction. It did not contain a completed future house waiting to arrive. Its finer continuation is being worked out through encounters, and those encounters can also interrupt it. Funding can disappear. A site can prove unsuitable. A builder can decline.

“Chain” names a path through this activity. Several exchanges can happen together, and later findings can revise earlier agreements. There is no requirement for a single tidy pipeline.

Return briefly to the telescope. Call the instrument M and the receiving person or detector C. M encounters the incoming light. C encounters the source through M, with M’s organization still contributing to what is received.

The mirror’s collecting area, the optical arrangement, and the detector’s response belong in the account. M is a participant in the supported encounter. The incoming relation and the receiving arrangement both contribute, although their roles and costs need not be equal.

At a coarser grain, we may describe M and C together as one receiving system. That grouping is useful when it preserves the constraints that matter. Calling them one cannot make the instrument’s contribution disappear.

The earlier Stage article develops the encounter itself. Here, we are following how its participants and results become available again.

This is where reserved coarseness becomes precise.

The participating domains themselves carry established constraints alongside open possibilities. Money has conditions on its availability and use. A plan holds some decisions while leaving others outstanding. A connection to a builder carries experience, access, trust, and limits. A tool brings capabilities that fit some tasks and fail at others.

These relations compose the project. They help determine what the project can become.

“Build a modest house beside this lake within this amount” can be a strong constraint. It still permits different room layouts, materials, and sequences of work. Coarse means those finer distinctions remain open relative to the present question. The constraint can be exact about what it does hold.

Douglas Engelbart approached practical capability through a related organizational question in his 1962 report: consider the person together with tools, language, methods, and training. His imagined architect develops a design through an arrangement that supports inspection and revision. That is a useful precedent for examining the whole working arrangement. Engelbart’s original report.

The funded plan also makes three conditions easier to separate. A house can be represented in a sketch. A plan can become established for reuse, so later decisions reliably begin from it. Calling a domain independently seated requires a further account of which dependencies it can carry through its own supported relations. Stability inside a host alone does not establish that stronger condition.

Those conditions cannot be collapsed into one another. An agreement maintained by people and records can be consequential while still depending on them. Within the framework, hosted logic also has its own incoming consequences and outgoing constraints at the grain where it participates. Its activity is already part of the situation.

Now put a hammer on the workbench.

Manufacturing it required many particular things to hold. The head needed a usable shape and material condition. The handle needed to fit and remain attached. A collection became a tool because its organization could support the work expected of it.

That establishment can be fine relative to making the hammer. For the house project, the resulting hammer can enter as one coarse capability: a usable tool for driving or pulling nails.

The manufacturer did not have to specify every nail it would meet, every hand that would hold it, or every repair it might help complete.

What resolves in one encounter can become coarse ground for another.

The hammer’s internal structure continues to matter. If the handle loosens, a distinction previously left in the background becomes consequential again. Coarse reuse depends on enough of that established structure continuing to hold.

The house can eventually do the same. Once built, it supplies ground for living, working, repairing, and rearranging. Its completion opens questions that the construction plan never individually settled.

This changes capacity as well as viewpoint.

In the framework, a common rule of primitive participation does not give every arbitrarily named domain an identical effective allowance. A composition includes members, relations among members, and established relations that can themselves participate. Reusing that organization changes how much relational work the arrangement can support.

Naming a collection “one” creates no extra capacity. Its organization has to carry the consequences. Adding relations can also introduce conflicts and obligations.

Nor does visible size tell us everything about the organization available. Dense relations can be carried locally. A domain can be richly organized inside while acting as one coarse participant in another encounter. Coarseness and relational density answer different questions.

Inherited support extends this beyond the workbench. The framework’s proposed gravity correspondence gives a large anchored domain a role in shared persistence: members can reuse common support instead of each separately carrying the whole relation to the outside. An Earth-like domain is the intended physical example. A nearby object’s participation can draw on that larger organization while contributing at a much coarser grain. The quantitative mapping to physical gravity remains a candidate.

If the same scale contribution supports two rulers, it may cancel from their ratio. That cancellation leaves the shared support in place. The comparison has simply stopped displaying it as a separate factor.

We also have to keep three questions distinct: how a relation traverses supported ground, how frequencies compare between domains, and how much total resolving capacity a composition carries. Greater capacity alone does not establish a faster traversal rate or a particular clock reading.

The same recursive question reaches meaning.

Consider a writer and a reader. The writer works through a language, a genre, a set of questions, and some expectation of possible readers. Those relations already shape which sentences get written. The text then encounters a reader whose memories and current questions differ from the writer’s.

A passage can become useful in a way neither side specified alone. It might give the reader a distinction they needed, or turn an old question into a new one. That new distinction can then participate in another conversation or decision.

This is what I mean here by Public Ciphertext, Private Punchline. The words are publicly available; a particular payoff can depend on the ground brought into the encounter. It is a metaphor for that relation, without requiring an encrypted message.

There is also a question about production and encounter, before the reader reaches the page. Conditionally within the framework, overlapping coarse projections can help shape a work and the supported routes by which it becomes available. Several concerns may meet in one story, and several readers may find different continuations through it. That does not require the work to specify one exclusive recipient.

The projection remains present and coarse. A writer’s anticipated reader is a current representation that can guide the writing. It is not a completed future person acting backward. Other participating constraints still affect what gets produced, whether it circulates, and whether a particular encounter happens at all. Possibility alone guarantees none of those steps.

The point reaches beyond interpreting something after its arrival. What is already supported can help form the next work, the routes to it, and what becomes possible when it is encountered.

These are differentiated encounters within one continuing relational ground. Each can have a local anchor without making that anchor a universal spatial center or beginning a separate world from zero.

The telescope inherits an organized receiving surface. The house project inherits plans, agreements, materials, and tools. The reader inherits language and a text, then may establish something that another encounter can use.

Look again at the hammer. Its manufacture resolved enough for it to become dependable ground. The project beside it still has decisions to make.

That is how established work and open possibility can belong to the same world.

Perception is part of what happens. What it resolves becomes part of what can happen next.

item.title: Why Does Heat Draw a Curve?
item.description: One comparison gives a contribution. A changing comparison traces the spectrum.
item.dc:creator: Soutame
item.content:encoded:
Image Caption: One thermal source, a changing range of comparison. The windows are a visual metaphor for selecting different grains; they are not a proposed instrument or experimental evidence for the framework.

A heating element can be giving off radiation while it still looks dark.

A slide in composition of explanation. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_af4Tc6gWmc6dGXrBcQtfUgue7Nfd6jx/view?usp=sharing


A thermal camera can already detect its infrared emission. Keep heating it and a visible glow appears. Our eyes have started catching part of what the element emits. NASA’s introduction to infrared shows this distinction between warm objects and visible glowing.

But the glow hides a question.

Imagine holding the element at a steady temperature and measuring its radiation through a sequence of narrow frequency ranges. How much arrives here? Then here? Then a little further along?

For the clean ideal thermal case, the readings rise, reach a peak, and fall. They do not give one isolated colour, and they do not give every range an equal share.

Why that shape?

Start with an ideal blackbody in thermal equilibrium. It absorbs incident radiation completely. A small opening into a cavity held at one temperature approximates it: incoming radiation is trapped and absorbed, while escaping radiation approaches the equilibrium spectrum. Temperature sets the ideal distribution. NRAO develops this physical setting.

An actual heating element brings its material response too. Its efficiency of emission can vary with wavelength. NIST measures that property by comparing a sample’s spectral radiance with a blackbody reference. Two surfaces at the same temperature need not give identical spectra. The reference and the material response have separate jobs in that measurement.

The blackbody is useful because it gives us a precise case to understand before adding those differences.

In the standard explanation, three things meet. There are available radiation modes: possible patterns of the field. Each photon carries energy proportional to its frequency. And thermal equilibrium determines the average occupation of the modes. Higher frequencies offer more modes per equal frequency interval, but their larger energy steps become harder to occupy at a given temperature. Eventually that suppression wins, and the spectrum falls. Planck’s law quantifies the balance. NRAO gives the mode counting and thermal derivation.

So physics already answers the opening question. The rise and fall express a changing balance between available modes, energy, and occupation across frequency.

There is also a small measurement detail that matters more than it first sounds.

A spectrum has a horizontal coordinate and a rule for how much interval each reading represents. Suppose we collect radiation from 1 to 2 micrometres, then from 2 to 3 micrometres. Both wavelength bins are one micrometre wide. Using the rounded speed of light, the first spans about 300 to 150 terahertz; the second spans about 150 to 100 terahertz. Their frequency widths are 150 and 50 terahertz.

Equal wavelength buckets can cover very unequal frequency ranges.

To preserve the same amount of radiation in matching intervals, the density must include that width conversion. Consequently, a plot per unit wavelength can peak at a different place from a plot per unit frequency. Relabelling the horizontal axis alone is insufficient. MIT’s notes show the factor connecting the two Planck densities.

That is a change in accounting. Changing a graph’s buckets does not create radiation in the element.

Now we can make the framework’s question precise enough to be useful.

Could a repeated relational operation supply a rule for the contribution at each selected comparison, with the changing comparison producing the whole spectrum?

The framework calls the selected level of distinction a grain. Here, that means which periodic distinctions the encounter requires. A broader grain can still be a definite, supported relation. It need not be a blurred version of a finished fine picture.

In the proposed account, the receiver and target meet at a selected grain. The contribution depends on that relation and on the support that remains consequential to it. Move through a range of grains and the supported result can change. Measured frequency is the physical label that this candidate account must eventually recover from the comparison.

This is a proposal about the encounter itself. It does not require a human watching, or a detector whose settings can dictate any answer it likes.

Before giving the operation a formula, try two ordinary sums.

At one selected comparison, suppose each further contribution has half the weight of the previous level. Starting with a first weight of one-half, we get:

1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1.

Now move to a different comparison. Its local factor is one-quarter:

1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + ... = 1/3.

Both use repeated proportions. Their totals differ because the selected comparison supplies a different proportion.

So when we say the factor is constant, what is being held still?

The factor stays fixed while we add repeats at one selected grain. The grain can then change, and its local factor can change with it.

There are two movements here. Moving along the sum asks what the next repeat contributes. Moving along the spectrum asks which comparison we are summing at.

We can hold the first rule steady locally while the second moves continuously. There is no need for one universal multiplier across the entire curve.

The fractions are model weights. They are not measured absorption probabilities or pieces of a photon. Identifying what physical relation supplies them is part of the proposed mechanism.

For the simple calculation, assume that the contributions are nonnegative and additive, that the first is weighted by q, and that every further repeat has the same factor q, with 0 < q < 1. Let the idealized sequence continue indefinitely. Then:

q+q2+q3+⋯=q1−q.

The familiar exponential enters through a change of notation. Define chi = -ln(q). Then q = exp(-chi), and:

q1−q=1exp⁡(χ)−1.

That equality is exact. The minus one follows from the continuing proportional sum.

The exponential describes how successive terms depend on the repeat index. It has not yet told us how the selected grain determines chi, or why chi should equal a measured frequency divided by a thermal scale.

The same caution applies to a shrinking-length picture. If a scalar length changes proportionally to its current length, integrating a specified proportional rate gives an exponential of accumulated change. A varying rate can go inside that accumulation. Choosing the base e does not choose the rate, identify an outside clock, or establish that length contraction and spectral occupation are the same operation.

The useful result is narrower and more concrete: a local proportional repeat rule supplies this denominator. A separate weighting still has to specify what the observable counts.

For the conventional Planck frequency shape, let x = h nu/(k_B T), where nu is frequency, T is absolute temperature, h is Planck’s constant, and k_B is Boltzmann’s constant. At fixed temperature, removing the dimensional prefactor leaves:

Sν(x)=x3[e−x+e−2x+e−3x+⋯]=x3ex−1.

Here we have supplied two conventional inputs: chi = x and the weighting x^3. In ordinary physics, mode counting supplies two powers of frequency and energy per photon supplies the third. In the framework construction, those physical identifications remain to be derived.

Image Caption: Calculated illustration. Left: unweighted sums at local ratios of one-half and one-quarter. Right: the conditional Planck shape per unit frequency at fixed temperature, using the conventional inputs x = h nu/(k_B T) and x^3, normalized to a peak of one. Colours separate mathematical terms. They are not measured components, individual colours of light, or physical layers.

This is more informative than merely drawing a hump that resembles a thermal curve. The sum reproduces the stated shape exactly under its inputs. It also lets us see which terms matter where.

At small x, the local factor is close to one. Later terms diminish slowly, so many repeats contribute. At large x, the factor is small. Later terms disappear rapidly and the first carries nearly the whole response. The weighting and the repeat sum together determine the rise, the peak, and the tail.

But the repetition assumption must stay attached to the result.

If the factor changes between repeats at the same grain, the weights become q_1, then q_1 q_2, then q_1 q_2 q_3, and so on. Each term contains the product of the factors actually encountered. Their sum need not have the simple denominator above.

And additive weights cannot silently replace coherent wave amplitudes. Phase relations and interference must be accounted for whenever they matter. Piling sine waves together to draw an instantaneous waveform would answer a different question from the spectral distribution considered here.

There is a useful way to test what this rule contributes. Keep the conventional inputs, but stop the mathematical sum after N terms.

Far enough toward small x—specifically, when x is much smaller than 1/N—each retained exponential is close to one. There are only N of them, so the weighted response approaches N x^3. With the infinite sum, the low end instead approaches x^2.

Stopping the sum changes the low-frequency rise. It is not merely a brightness adjustment. At large x, both versions are still dominated by the first term.

That is a diagnostic within the model. It does not show that physical radiation has a finite repeat cutoff, and finite resolving capacity does not by itself establish such a cutoff. The repeat index has not been identified with a count of separately rendered physical events.

The distinction between shape and calibration matters too. One constant can raise or lower a curve without changing its shape. Changing the grain dependence of the weights can change the shape itself. Changing spectral bins adds its own conversion: per logarithmic frequency interval, the conventional numerator becomes x^4. A constant multiplier cannot replace those operations.

The framework’s comparison also has to keep its support attached. Target, receiver, and any anchor relation that changes the result belong in the comparison. Truly common factors may cancel. Support that distinguishes the two sides cannot disappear into shorthand. Its budget means resolving capacity; it is not another name for heat, photon energy, or clock time.

This leaves a specific piece of work to do. The algebra is available. The candidate is that supported repeated resolution supplies the weights. A native physical account must identify those contributions and recover the argument, frequency weighting, absolute normalization, and scaling between differently supported grounds. The older square-root toy remains a separate illustration; this sum does not retrospectively turn it into Planck’s law.

That status is the one preserved in the current spectrum source and its grain-sweep extension.

The related cooling question comes afterward: how does the spectrum compare when the participating grounds change? That is the question carried by the CMB episode.

Article Slot: URL: https://soutame.substack.com/p/the-cmb-is-losing-the-resolution

Return to the heating element, held steady while we work through its radiation.

Each point on the graph belongs to a selected range and a declared way of counting. Under the candidate repeat rule, one comparison lets many terms matter; another leaves almost everything to the first. Moving through the range gathers those different outcomes into one curve.

The glow now carries a more precise question: what rule determines the contribution here, and how does that rule change when the comparison moves?

The sweep makes the curve. The continuation rule gives it a shape.
